title: WAF killswitch hits latent Lua nil bug, 500s on 28% of traffic
trigger: While mitigating CVE-2025-55182, Cloudflare raised the WAF body buffer to 1MB and used a global killswitch to disable an internal WAF test ruleset that could not handle the larger size.
impact: For about 25 minutes, from 08:47 to 09:12 UTC, roughly 28% of Cloudflare HTTP traffic, sites on the FL1 proxy using the Managed Ruleset, got HTTP 500 errors on nearly every request.
detection: Automated alerts fired and an incident was declared at 08:50 UTC.
fix: The configuration change was reverted at 09:11 UTC, and Cloudflare committed to gradual rollouts for security config, fail-open data plane handling, easier break-glass access and a network change freeze.
summary: Responding to a React Server Components vulnerability, Cloudflare enlarged the WAF request-body buffer and switched off an internal testing ruleset through its killswitch, a change that spreads fleet-wide instantly. In the older FL1 proxy, skipping that rule meant its execute object was never built, and later Lua code indexed it anyway, throwing an attempt to index a nil value error. Affected sites served HTTP 500 for nearly all requests for 25 minutes. The Rust FL2 proxy did not have the bug.

title: Oversized Bot Management feature file crashes Cloudflare's proxy
trigger: A ClickHouse permissions change exposed extra table metadata, so the query building the Bot Management feature file returned duplicate rows and roughly doubled the file.
impact: Core CDN and security traffic returned 5xx errors from about 11:20 UTC, with Access, Turnstile, Workers KV, the dashboard and Email Security also hit; main impact ended at 14:30 and full recovery came at 17:06 UTC.
detection: An automated test flagged the problem at 11:31 UTC and an incident call opened at 11:35, with the team first suspecting a DDoS attack.
fix: Engineers stopped generating new feature files, pushed a known-good file globally and restarted the proxy, then planned to validate internal config like user input, add kill switches and review proxy failure modes.
summary: A database access change at Cloudflare made a ClickHouse query that builds the Bot Management feature file return duplicate columns from a second schema. The bigger file exceeded the 200-feature limit preallocated by the Rust FL2 proxy, causing a panic and HTTP 5xx errors across the network, while legacy FL returned zero bot scores. Because ClickHouse nodes were updated gradually, good and bad files alternated every five minutes, making the outage flap and look like an attack. The independent status page coincidentally went down too.

title: AWS us-east-1 outage hits incident.io through third-party dependencies
trigger: The AWS us-east-1 outage broke a telecom provider and Docker Hub, which incident.io relied on even though its own platform runs on Google Cloud.
impact: SMS and phone on-call notifications were delayed from 07:20 to 09:26 UTC, SAML login was degraded for about two hours, the Scribe note taker could not join calls for several hours, and about 4% of status page traffic errored for 25 minutes.
detection: An on-call engineer was paged at 07:21 UTC for high SMS and phone error rates, and blackbox exporters in nine regions caught the status page errors.
fix: Once Docker Hub partly recovered the team shipped isolated notification queues and escalation fixes, then removed the Docker Hub dependency, added telecom redundancy and tuned Postgres autovacuum.
summary: When AWS us-east-1 failed, incident.io's GCP-hosted platform stayed up but its dependencies did not. A telecom provider outage plus aggressive client retries made notification jobs run up to 60 times longer, and shared queues delayed email, Slack and push alerts too. Fixes could not ship because the build used a Docker Hub base image. Dead tuples in a Postgres escalations index made lock acquisition eat nearly half of worker capacity, and an internal rate limiter only applied to the top 10 organisations.

title: AWS outage and SDK retry flood disrupt LaunchDarkly flag delivery
trigger: The AWS us-east-1 outage degraded EC2, Lambda, DynamoDB and the Route 53 control plane, and a later internal change sent flag delivery onto a legacy path with cold caches.
impact: Service was disrupted for roughly 24 hours; US customers could not log in or manage flags, server-side SDK connection errors reached about 99% globally, and event ingestion lost data until 3:00 PM PT on October 20.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Streaming recovered by 12:05 AM PT on October 21 after load balancers were scaled out and flag delivery was decoupled from the web app; follow-ups include a new delivery architecture, streaming-to-polling SDK failover and moving DR tooling out of us-east-1.
summary: LaunchDarkly's outage had two phases. First, the AWS us-east-1 failure left its web app and API unable to autoscale, so US customers could not manage flags and client-side streaming stalled. Then, at 11:48 AM PT, a change meant to reduce web app load pushed the flag delivery network onto an old routing path with cold caches; SDKs retried heavily, overwhelming the streaming service and its load balancer, while ongoing EC2 capacity problems blocked scale-out until after midnight.

title: DynamoDB DNS automation race empties us-east-1 endpoint
trigger: A latent race condition between two DNS Enactor processes let a stale DNS plan overwrite a newer one, after which a cleanup job deleted it and removed every IP address for dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
impact: Over about 14.5 hours in US-EAST-1, clients could not connect to DynamoDB for roughly three hours, EC2 launches failed with capacity errors, some Network Load Balancers returned connection errors, and Lambda, ECS, EKS, Amazon Connect, STS, IAM console sign-in and Redshift were degraded.
detection: Engineering teams engaged as soon as errors started and traced the problem to DynamoDB DNS state by 12:38 AM PDT; NLB health check problems were caught by monitoring at 6:52 AM.
fix: Operators manually restored the DNS records, restarted EC2 droplet lease managers and throttled requests to drain backlogs, and temporarily disabled NLB health-check failover; AWS turned off the DNS automation worldwide until the race is fixed and added velocity limits for NLB capacity removal.
summary: A timing bug in DynamoDB's automated DNS management in US-EAST-1 published an empty record set for the regional endpoint, so anything resolving it got no addresses. The outage rippled into EC2, whose droplet lease manager depends on DynamoDB and fell into a congestive backlog that blocked new instance launches. Network propagation delays then made NLB health checks fail healthy targets. Lambda, container services, Amazon Connect and sign-in all suffered, and some Redshift clusters took until the next day to recover.

title: Dashboard React bug floods Tenant Service, breaking API auth
trigger: A dashboard release with a React useEffect whose dependency array held an object rebuilt on every render kept calling the /organizations endpoint, colliding with a Tenant Service deploy.
impact: From 17:57 to 19:12 UTC the Cloudflare dashboard was heavily degraded and the API failed with 5xx errors in two windows, while CDN and edge security traffic were unaffected.
detection: Automated alerting paged the right engineers, who also saw rising Tenant Service and API traffic.
fix: Engineers applied a global rate limit, added Tenant Service pods, reverted a bad patch and hotfixed the dashboard, then planned Argo Rollouts, jittered retries, more capacity and retry tagging.
summary: A Cloudflare dashboard release included a React useEffect hook that re-ran on every render because an object in its dependency list was recreated each time, firing repeated calls to /organizations plus retries. The extra load overwhelmed the Tenant Service, a Go service on Kubernetes that is part of API authorization, so authorization could not be evaluated and APIs returned 5xx errors. An attempted fix that removed some error handling made things worse, causing a second outage window until it was reverted.

title: One customer's traffic surge congests Cloudflare-AWS links in Ashburn
trigger: One customer in AWS us-east-1 requested so many cached objects that the response traffic saturated Cloudflare's direct peering links with AWS in Ashburn.
impact: Customers whose origins were in AWS us-east-1 saw high latency, packet loss, timeouts and failures reaching origins from 16:27 UTC until about 20:18 UTC, while Cloudflare's other services were unaffected.
detection: Cloudflare's network team was alerted to Ashburn congestion at 16:44 UTC and opened a customer-impact incident at 17:45 UTC, with latency SLO probes also tracking the degradation.
fix: Cloudflare rate-limited the customer and re-engineered traffic while AWS reverted its BGP withdrawals, and follow-ups include per-customer traffic budgets, faster interconnect upgrades and coordinated traffic engineering with AWS.
summary: A surge of requests from one customer in AWS us-east-1 roughly doubled Cloudflare-to-AWS traffic and filled the direct peering links in Ashburn, one of which was already running at half capacity. AWS withdrew some BGP prefixes to relieve the links, pushing traffic onto an offsite interconnect that also saturated, and Ashburn edge routers dropped high-priority packets. Customers with AWS-hosted origins saw timeouts and slow responses for almost four hours until rate limiting and route normalization.

title: Salesloft Drift OAuth theft exposes Cloudflare support cases
trigger: After breaching Salesloft, threat actor GRUB1 used stolen OAuth credentials from the Drift chatbot's Salesforce integration to log into Cloudflare's Salesforce tenant.
impact: The text of Salesforce support case objects, including customer contact details and any secrets customers had pasted into tickets, was bulk-exported, and 104 Cloudflare API tokens were found in the stolen data; Cloudflare's own systems and network were not breached.
detection: Salesforce and Salesloft notified Cloudflare on August 23, 2025, several days after the last attacker activity on August 17.
fix: Cloudflare disabled the Drift integration and revoked its client ID and secrets, removed Salesloft software, disconnected and re-onboarded all Salesforce integrations with new secrets, rotated the 104 exposed API tokens, and told customers to rotate any credentials shared in support cases.
summary: In August 2025 an attacker Cloudflare calls GRUB1, armed with OAuth credentials stolen from the Salesloft Drift integration, accessed Cloudflare's Salesforce tenant on August 12, ran reconnaissance, then used a Bulk API 2.0 job on August 17 to export the text of its support cases. Those cases could include API tokens, passwords and logs customers had pasted in. Cloudflare scanned the data, rotated 104 Cloudflare API tokens, cut off the Drift integration, rotated third-party credentials, and urged customers to rotate anything shared via support.

title: Workers KV storage outage cascades to Access, WARP and more
trigger: The central storage backing Workers KV, part of which runs on a third-party cloud provider, failed when that provider had its own outage.
impact: For about two and a half hours, roughly 90% of Workers KV requests failed and dependent products broke globally, including 100% of Access identity logins, WARP registrations, Gateway proxying, dashboard logins, Workers AI, Stream and Pages builds.
detection: The WARP team saw device registration failures at 17:52 UTC and declared an incident, and Access error-rate alerts and SLO drops followed at 18:05 UTC.
fix: Teams degraded features that depended on KV and prepared an alternate datastore until the storage recovered, then committed to removing single-provider dependence for KV, moving critical namespaces to Cloudflare infrastructure and limiting per-product blast radius.
summary: Workers KV relies on a central source-of-truth store, part of which was hosted by a third-party cloud that suffered an outage. With that store unavailable, KV cold reads and writes failed, and because many Cloudflare products are built on KV, the failure spread: Access identity logins, WARP sign-ups, Gateway, dashboard login, Turnstile, Workers AI, Stream, Images and Pages all saw heavy errors. No data was lost. Service returned when the storage recovered, followed by cache repopulation errors.

title: Blank policy fields crash Google Service Control in every region
trigger: A quota policy record with unintended blank fields was written to Spanner and replicated globally, hitting an unguarded null pointer in a new Service Control quota check added on May 29.
impact: Google Cloud and Workspace external APIs and consoles returned elevated 503 errors worldwide for about three hours across roughly 100 Cloud and 10 Workspace products, with us-central1 and some products such as Vertex AI recovering later.
detection: SRE triage started within two minutes and the root cause was found in about ten, but the status dashboard was itself down so the first public notice took about an hour.
fix: A kill switch disabling the faulty code path was rolled out in about 40 minutes, task creation was throttled in us-central1, and follow-ups include fail-open checks, feature flags on critical binaries and randomized exponential backoff.
summary: Service Control, the binary that enforces API policy and quota across Google Cloud, gained a new quota check in May with no error handling and no feature flag. On June 12 a policy update with blank fields replicated globally through Spanner within seconds, the check dereferenced a null pointer, and Service Control crash-looped in every region. External API calls to Cloud and Workspace failed with 503s. In us-central1, restarting tasks without backoff overloaded the Spanner table they relied on, slowing recovery further.

title: PGAudit hang during migration locks incident.io database
trigger: A routine migration adding an empty table and an index ran shortly after a Postgres 17 upgrade, and the re-enabled PGAudit extension froze while holding critical locks.
impact: The dashboard, mobile app, Slack app and API were slow or timing out for about 11 minutes, including a 2-minute full primary database outage, though on-call alerts and escalations were still delivered.
detection: Monitoring alerted the team quickly.
fix: Because the stuck PGAudit processes ignored kill signals, the team restarted the database and then disabled and removed PGAudit, with further root-cause investigation and monitoring improvements planned.
summary: A few days after upgrading to Postgres 17, incident.io ran an ordinary schema migration. The PGAudit logging extension, switched back on after the upgrade, interacted badly with the migration and stopped responding while holding locks, so other queries piled up behind it. Users saw intermittent slowness and timeouts across the web dashboard, mobile and Slack apps, and API. Terminating the stuck backends did not work, so engineers restarted the primary database, causing two minutes of full downtime, and then removed PGAudit.

title: Stale stats after Postgres upgrade delay CircleCI workflows
trigger: A blue/green upgrade of the workflows service database ran ANALYZE before a second major version upgrade in the same rollout, leaving planner statistics stale.
impact: For about 1 hour 37 minutes, starting and cancelling workflows and jobs was slow or failed, some jobs were dropped after 10 minutes of retries, and the workflows UI was hard to use.
detection: Rising latency and job errors were spotted at 22:17 UTC and a public incident was declared at 22:35 UTC.
fix: After restarting pods and upsizing the database did not help, the team re-enabled writes on the old database and made it primary again, and now runs statistics analysis after every major version change with extra tests and checkpoints before cutover.
summary: CircleCI upgraded the Postgres database behind its workflows service using a blue/green deployment that included two major version jumps. Table statistics were rebuilt after the first jump only, so after the second the query planner made poor choices and queries went to disk. Workflow starts and cancellations slowed, some jobs were dropped, and the UI struggled to show workflows. Restoring the previous database as primary ended the incident. The report's date is inconsistent, citing both April 3 and April 4.

title: Manual WAF rule change blocks CircleCI UI and builds
trigger: An operator who thought they were doing read-only security checks edited a WAF rule by hand, possible because an IAM role could bypass the Terraform pipeline, and the rule blocked legitimate traffic.
impact: From 00:16 to 01:49 UTC, about 1 hour 33 minutes, customers could not load the CircleCI UI or start builds, as traffic to the api.circleci.com and circleci.com CloudFront distributions was blocked.
detection: Monitoring flagged degraded services from 00:26, but the cause was only found at 01:35 when automated Terraform drift detection reported the WAF difference, nearly 80 minutes after the change.
fix: The rule was reverted on both CloudFront distributions at 01:41; follow-ups include tighter IAM policies blocking out-of-band changes, faster drift alerts, WAF rule testing and monitoring, and organization-wide Security Control Policies.
summary: On April 4, 2025 CircleCI's UI and build triggering failed for about 93 minutes after an operator, believing they were only reading configuration, manually altered a Web Application Firewall rule that then blocked real traffic to its CloudFront distributions. An IAM misconfiguration let that role skip Terraform. Responders were slowed by an unrelated incident ending at the same time and by assuming WAF changes always went through Terraform; drift detection eventually pinpointed the rule, which was reverted. CircleCI tightened IAM and WAF change controls.

title: R2 credential rotation sent to wrong Worker environment
trigger: During a credential rotation for the R2 Gateway Worker, the new secret was deployed without the --env flag, landing in a non-production Worker before the old credentials were deleted.
impact: For 67 minutes, from 21:38 to 22:45 UTC, all R2 writes and about 35% of reads failed globally, and Images, Stream and Vectorize uploads failed completely, with log delivery delayed up to 70 minutes.
detection: R2 global availability alerts fired at 21:45 UTC and an incident was declared at 21:50, though the gradual decline delayed diagnosis.
fix: Engineers deployed the credentials to the production Worker at 22:45 UTC, and added credential ID logging, a check before deleting old keys, tooling that enforces environment selection and two-person review.
summary: Cloudflare engineers rotating the storage credentials used by the R2 Gateway Worker ran wrangler secret put and wrangler deploy without specifying --env, so the new secret went to the default, non-production Worker. Once the old key was deleted, production R2 could no longer authenticate to storage. Writes failed outright and reads partly failed, cascading to Images, Stream, Vectorize, Cache Reserve, log delivery and billing downloads. A first retry repeated the same mistake; release history review finally exposed the wrong target. No data was lost.

title: Faulty Falcon content update crashes Windows hosts worldwide
trigger: A Rapid Response Content update, Channel File 291, supplied 21 input fields to a sensor template expecting 20, causing an out-of-bounds memory read in the Falcon Windows sensor.
impact: Windows hosts running Falcon sensor 7.11 or later that were online between 04:09 and 05:27 UTC crashed with blue screens, and recovery took days, with about 99% of sensors back online by July 29.
detection: Not stated in detail; the hub says the problem was identified quickly and the file was reverted 78 minutes after release.
fix: CrowdStrike reverted the channel file and guided manual and later automated host remediation, then added field-count validation, Content Interpreter bounds checks, staged deployment rings and customer control over content rollout.
summary: CrowdStrike released a Rapid Response Content file for its Falcon Windows sensor that provided one more input field than the sensor's Content Interpreter expected. A bug in the Content Validator let it through, and the mismatch caused an out-of-bounds read that crashed Windows into a blue screen on every affected host that was online during a 78-minute window. Mac and Linux were unaffected. Many machines needed hands-on fixes such as booting to recovery and deleting the channel file.

title: New DDoS rule triggers infinite Lua loop, pinning edge CPUs
trigger: A gradually deployed DDoS mitigation rule that rate-limited by cookie value hit a latent bug in the legacy rate-limiting code when clients sent mixed valid and invalid cookies.
impact: For 114 minutes, many data centers served errors to 1.4-2.1% of CDN requests at peak, with total 5xx reaching 3.45% and p99 time to first byte roughly tripling.
detection: An incident was opened automatically at 18:04 UTC when global CPU load stayed high, though engineers first blamed a concurrent backbone congestion event.
fix: Engineers ran mass rolling restarts, fixed a Traffic Manager bug, and disabled the rule, then planned to replace the legacy rate limiter and guard against endless tail-call loops.
summary: A new Cloudflare DDoS rule keyed rate limits on cookies, and its key-generation function ended up calling itself. Two cookie validity checks disagreed when a request had several cookies, so the function recursed forever; Lua proper tail calls kept the stack flat, meaning no overflow error ever surfaced and the process just spun at 100% CPU. One bad request poisoned a worker, and load shifted by Unimog and Traffic Manager spread failures between servers and data centers, raising error rates and latency worldwide.

title: Second Portland power loss tests Code Orange failover work
trigger: Four facility circuit switchboards at the Flexential PDX01 site failed together, reportedly because breaker trip settings were too low, taking out both primary and redundant power to all Cloudflare cages.
impact: Control plane APIs and dashboards recovered in about seven minutes, but analytics stayed down until later that day; the edge network serving traffic was unaffected.
detection: Loss of connectivity to PDX01 triggered alerts immediately, and a total facility power loss was confirmed shortly after.
fix: Over 100 databases across more than 20 clusters failed over automatically to other Portland sites, Flexential reset and corrected the switchboards, and the top follow-up is finishing high availability for the analytics platform and eliminating remaining manual steps.
summary: Five months after a similar outage, another full power failure hit a Cloudflare core facility in Portland when four circuit switchboards tripped at once. This time the control plane failed over on its own within minutes, thanks to work done under the Code Orange program: HA database topology, pre-provisioned capacity elsewhere, and Logpush failover to Amsterdam. Analytics, which still depended on the lost facility, was the main gap. Cold-starting the site took around 10 hours versus roughly 72 previously.

title: Empty backup ID mixes free-tier database data in shared storage
trigger: A buggy migration left some databases with an empty backup identifier, so their backups pointed at one shared storage path, and databases recreated from it after scale-to-zero picked up others' data.
impact: About 0.07% of managed databases were affected: from 1 to 4 December 2023 they could see data from the shared location, and the fix rolled them back to 1 December backups, losing later writes.
detection: An external researcher reported the leak at 8:10 AM UTC on 4 December 2023.
fix: Turso patched the bug about an hour later, reran the migration with correct parameters and restored affected databases under correct IDs, and planned per-database backup isolation, ownership checks and safer migrations.
summary: Turso free-tier databases scale to zero after an hour idle. A configuration change shipped on 20 November contained a migration bug that blanked the backup identifier for some databases, pointing their backups at a common bucket path. When fly.io lacked resources to restart such a database, Turso rebuilt it from that shared location, so customers could read data belonging to other databases. After a researcher reported it, Turso fixed the bug, restored from 1 December backups, and accepted the resulting data loss.

title: Data center power loss takes down control plane and analytics
trigger: Utility maintenance and a suspected transformer ground fault cut both grid and generator power at the Flexential PDX-04 facility in Oregon, and its UPS batteries ran out after roughly four minutes.
impact: The Cloudflare dashboard, APIs and analytics were degraded for about 41 hours, raw logs were unavailable for most customers for the whole event and much Logpush data was lost, while edge traffic kept flowing.
detection: Alerts fired when the two routers linking PDX-04 dropped offline at 11:44 UTC; the earlier switch to generator power went unnoticed and the facility operator did not notify Cloudflare until 12:28 UTC.
fix: Cloudflare failed control plane services over to European disaster recovery sites, rate limited a thundering herd of API retries, and rebuilt PDX-04 servers from scratch, then launched a Code Orange program to remove single-facility dependencies and test full data center loss.
summary: A power event at a single Portland-area colocation facility knocked out Cloudflare's control plane and analytics for roughly two days. Services labeled highly available still relied on Kafka and ClickHouse clusters that lived only in PDX-04, and losing an entire facility had never been rehearsed. Customers saw dashboard and API errors, missing analytics and dropped log pushes while proxy traffic stayed up. Recovery required a failover to Europe and a slow, full re-bootstrap of every server in the building.

title: Workers KV rollback points production at a staging build
trigger: While rolling back a KV release, a deployment tool bug that listed staging and production releases together pointed production at a version only deployed to staging.
impact: For 37 minutes, from 19:54 to 20:31 UTC, KV returned HTTP 401 errors, breaking Pages, Access logins, WARP device posture, Workers edits, Turnstile, Images, AI Gateway and the dashboard.
detection: Automated alerting fired right after traffic began being misrouted.
fix: Engineers used break-glass procedures to repoint production to the previous good build, and planned standardized deployments, Access-independent rollbacks, input validation and environment checks.
summary: A progressive rollout of a new Cloudflare Workers KV build hit a routing problem, so the team rolled back. A latent bug in the deployment tool mixed staging and production releases, so the rollback targeted a script that ran nowhere in production, black-holing traffic and making KV answer reads and writes with HTTP 401. Pages sites returned 500, Access logins and posture checks failed, Turnstile failed closed, and internal tooling broke because it depended on KV via Access, slowing the manual fix.

title: Unparseable ZONEMD record leaves 1.1.1.1 on stale, expired root zone
trigger: The DNS root zone began carrying a ZONEMD record on 21 September, which Cloudflare's root zone parser could not handle, so updates silently stopped loading.
impact: From 07:00 to about 10:32 UTC, the 1.1.1.1 resolver returned SERVFAIL for valid lookups, peaking at 15% of queries versus a 3% baseline, affecting WARP, Zero Trust and downstream resolvers.
detection: Users reported unexpected SERVFAIL responses starting 07:57 UTC and an incident was declared at 08:03 UTC.
fix: Engineers stopped 1.1.1.1 from preloading the root zone at 10:30 UTC, and planned stale-zone alerts, ingestion that tolerates new record types, parse-failure tests and a cap on stale zone use per RFC 8806.
summary: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 resolver serves a local copy of the DNS root zone through a static_zone component that only swaps in a new version after a clean parse. When the root zone added a ZONEMD record, parsing failed and the 21 September copy stayed in use for two weeks. Its DNSSEC signatures expired on 4 October, so validation broke and resolvers returned SERVFAIL, mostly in large sites like Ashburn, Frankfurt and Singapore. An initial override rule failed because a tag was not forwarded between cache nodes.

title: Connection churn on GKE node causes Postgres and memcached timeouts
trigger: A recent change with an accidental database join made the app fire thousands of duplicate calls to an external third party, flooding a node with short-lived connections.
impact: Postgres connection timeouts spiked and a small share of requests hit memcached i/o timeouts over several days; the post gives no precise duration or user count, and the incident date is not stated beyond the September 2023 publication.
detection: An incident was declared after a spike in Postgres connection timeouts, with new connections being opened at hundreds per second.
fix: The team fixed the accidental join, lengthened connection lifetimes, used static pool sizes and more idle memcached connections, and plans to cap outbound concurrency and use keep-alives.
summary: Soon after moving to Google Kubernetes Engine, incident.io saw Postgres connection timeouts and sporadic memcached i/o timeouts. Connection pools were churning, reopening hundreds of connections per second, and a buggy join was making thousands of duplicate external API calls. The team's leading theory is that this burst of TCP connections drove up CPU in GKE Dataplane V2 anetd pods, dropping packets for other traffic on the same node. Deploying the join fix and stabilizing pools brought new Postgres connections down from about 200 to 1 per second.

title: Stuck cache writes trigger MySQL deadlock and full Honeycomb outage
trigger: After a routine switch between two Retriever clusters, the query engine stopped writing last-written timestamps the schema cache depended on, and a feature-flag bug kept writes disabled even after the flag was reverted.
impact: All of Honeycomb was down for about 68 minutes (13:40 to 14:48 UTC), with no ingest or querying, and data sent during the window was lost unless customers buffered it.
detection: A Shepherd SLO began burning slowly hours after the cluster switch, and the next morning charts showed the database update calls had stopped.
fix: Engineers tripped circuit breakers to shed Shepherd traffic, failed the locked MySQL primary over to a replica and manually refreshed schema timestamps; the cluster migration was finished and the code able to disable cache writes removed.
summary: Honeycomb moved traffic between Retriever clusters to dodge a bug, but the active cluster stopped updating last-written timestamps, weakening the Shepherd ingest schema cache. Flipping writes back with a feature flag failed because hosts told to stop writing never resumed until restarted, a flaw previously hidden by frequent deploys. As cache misses surged, reads piled onto the main MySQL database on RDS, a rare deadlock locked threads and exhausted connections, and every service failed. A failover to a replica restored the database.

title: Missing slash in redirect URL breaks all crates.io downloads
trigger: A refactor moving S3 access to the object_store crate dropped the slash between the CDN prefix and path, so download redirects pointed to the bogus host static.crates.iocrates.
impact: For about 13 minutes (12:17 to 12:30 UTC), every crate download failed, roughly 3.7 million failed requests at about 4,700 per second, and cargo users saw could not resolve host errors.
detection: The deploying developer saw elevated request rates in Grafana, and a community member reported the GitHub issue on Zulip about 11 minutes after deployment.
fix: The deploy was rolled back in the Heroku UI within about a minute, a corrected change with realistic tests shipped later, and crate downloads were added to the staging smoke test plan.
summary: A crates.io pull request finished migrating S3 access to the object_store crate and refactored how download endpoints build redirect URLs. Tests used values unlike production's environment variables, so nobody noticed that the slash between the CDN host and path was lost. After deploy, cargo was redirected to static.crates.iocrates/..., failed DNS lookups, and retried, producing millions of failed downloads. The change had merged without review and staging smoke tests covered publishing only. A Heroku rollback restored service.

title: Latent Lambda Frontend bug hit at new cell size in us-east-1
trigger: Routine daily scaling of the Lambda Frontend pushed one cell past a size it had never reached, exposing a latent defect in execution environment allocation.
impact: Lambda in US-EAST-1 returned elevated errors and latency for about 3 hours 48 minutes, and STS, AWS Sign-in, EventBridge, EKS, the Management Console, Amazon Connect and Support Center were degraded.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem; it says engineering teams engaged immediately and found the defect by 12:26 PM PDT.
fix: Engineers scaled the Frontend fleet back below the triggering size, which restored invocations, then disabled that scaling, fixed and deployed the bug fix to all Regions and planned to bound every cell to a tested size.
summary: As Lambda's Frontend fleet grew to meet normal afternoon traffic, one US-EAST-1 cell crossed a capacity threshold never seen before. A latent bug then caused execution environments to be allocated but never used, so Lambda could not provision environments for new invocations. Synchronous calls failed until about 1:45 PM PDT and async backlogs drained by 3:37 PM. Services built on Lambda, including STS, console sign-in and EventBridge, also saw errors.

title: Foreign key type overflow breaks Heroku logins and deploys
trigger: A foreign key column used a smaller integer type than the primary key it pointed to, and once the primary key outgrew it new authorizations failed.
impact: All customers were unable to log in or deploy for about 1 hour 45 minutes, followed by roughly 2 hours of full outage of the Heroku API, Dashboard and CLI; running apps stayed up.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem beyond a public notice at 15:57 UTC reporting global authentication failures, with users seeing HTTP 500 Application error pages.
fix: Engineers migrated the column to the correct type, which wiped Postgres statistics and slowed queries, so they ran the API read-only until statistics were rebuilt, and plan schema-mismatch monitoring, alerts on columns nearing type limits, and playbook updates to refresh statistics.
summary: Heroku's platform API went down when a primary key grew past the range of a narrower foreign key column referencing it, stopping new OAuth authorizations and therefore logins and deploys. Fixing the column type with a migration reset Postgres table statistics, and the resulting slow query plans escalated a partial failure into a full API, Dashboard and CLI outage. Running dynos were unaffected. Service returned once statistics were refreshed.

title: redis-py connection bug shows ChatGPT users other users' data
trigger: A server change at 1 a.m. Pacific raised Redis request cancellations, exposing a redis-py asyncio bug that left cancelled connections holding stale responses for the next request.
impact: Some users saw other users' chat titles, and payment details such as name, email, address and card last four digits of 1.2% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window may have been exposed; ChatGPT was taken offline and a few hours of history were lost.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: OpenAI took ChatGPT offline, patched redis-py with the Redis maintainers, added checks that cached data matches the requesting user, notified affected users and hardened its Redis Cluster.
summary: ChatGPT caches user data in Redis Cluster via the asyncio redis-py client. If a request was cancelled after being sent but before its reply was read, the pooled connection kept the orphaned reply and handed it to the next unrelated request. A change on March 20 sharply increased cancellations, so some users saw other people's conversation titles, and some subscription emails and account pages exposed other Plus users' names, emails, addresses and partial card details. Full card numbers were never exposed.

title: Kubernetes upgrade corrupts iptables, CircleCI jobs stop starting
trigger: An in-progress Kubernetes upgrade of the main production cluster led to kube-proxy sync failures that left iptables rules corrupted on many nodes.
impact: Docker, Machine, macOS and Windows jobs were delayed and then stopped starting, and the UI and API degraded, from about 18:00 UTC on March 14 until about 01:27 UTC on March 15, with follow-on RabbitMQ and GitHub checks problems later that day.
detection: Engineers noticed rising service-to-service communication errors around 18:00 UTC; the postmortem does not describe a specific alert.
fix: The team restarted services, every node and the rest of the infrastructure, then RabbitMQ nodes to clear corrupted queues, and added kube-proxy sync error alerts while reworking the upgrade process.
summary: During a Kubernetes version upgrade of CircleCI's main cluster, kube-proxy repeatedly failed to sync and left broken iptables rules on multiple nodes, causing widespread internal networking failures. Restarting node-local DNS and CoreDNS made name resolution fail entirely, and full recovery needed restarts of every node and later of RabbitMQ to fix corrupted queues. Jobs across executors stopped starting for about seven hours. The postmortem notes there was no single trigger.

title: Kubernetes 1.24 upgrade drops label, breaking Calico route reflectors
trigger: Upgrading the legacy Kubernetes cluster from 1.23 to 1.24 removed the node-role.kubernetes.io/master label that the Calico route reflector configuration selected on.
impact: Reddit was broken for 314 minutes on the afternoon of March 14 in US hours, with error pages or empty home feeds.
detection: The site halted about two minutes after the upgrade began and an incident was opened immediately; the cluster had lost its metrics, so engineers relied on CDN edge stats.
fix: After failing to fix forward, the team restored the control plane from backup, regenerated TLS certificates for a hostname mismatch, and ramped traffic back in steps; follow-ups target safer, more uniform cluster upgrades.
summary: On Pi Day 2023 an in-place upgrade of Reddit's largest, hand-built Kubernetes cluster to 1.24 knocked out pod networking. Calico route reflectors were configured years earlier to run on nodes carrying the master label, which 1.24 removes, so all routes dropped and in-cluster and Consul DNS stopped resolving. With no supported downgrade, engineers restored etcd from an outdated backup procedure, hit AWS instance capacity limits and certificate errors, then reopened traffic gradually from 1% to 100%.

title: Terraform deploy deletes static.crates.io DNS during cert swap
trigger: A single Terraform apply bundled a new CDN TLS certificate with DNS record changes, deleting the old records first and waiting about 10 minutes for the certificate before recreating them.
impact: For an estimated 10 to 15 minutes from about 09:15 UTC, static.crates.io failed to resolve, so Rust builds that needed to download crates failed, with some users affected longer due to resolver caching.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: The outage ended when Terraform recreated the DNS record, and the team committed to documenting deploys, shipping staged changes one at a time, and deploying on merge to avoid drift.
summary: crates.io infrastructure is managed with Terraform, and production lagged behind the main branch. A deploy therefore applied two separately tested changes together: a new TLS certificate for the CDN and updated DNS records. Terraform removed the existing certificate and DNS entries, spent around 10 minutes issuing the certificate, and only then wrote the new records. During that gap static.crates.io had no DNS entry, so cargo builds needing crate downloads failed until propagation finished around 09:40 UTC.

title: Access service token change blanks secrets, breaking many products
trigger: A release adding a last seen timestamp to Access service tokens wrote tokens back after reading them with the client secret redacted, saving empty secrets.
impact: For 121 minutes, from 17:50 to 19:51 UTC, WARP, Zero Trust, Gateway, R2, Cache Reserve, Cache Purge, Images and parts of the API failed, with Gateway peaking above 50,000 extra 5XX errors per minute.
detection: An internal alert fired when WARP device posture uploads fell to zero, followed by alerts from Cache Purge, R2, Images and Cache Reserve.
fix: Engineers restored correct token values for the affected internal accounts and then restored them from a database backup, and planned unit tests, auth failure alerts, faster table rollbacks and empty-string checks.
summary: A Cloudflare Access feature to show when service tokens were last used read each token through a path that redacts the client secret, then saved it, leaving an empty secret. A not-null constraint did not catch the empty string. Four internal accounts used by WARP, Gateway, R2, Cache Reserve, Cache Purge and Images lost working credentials as updates propagated, so devices failed posture checks and lost Internet access, R2 requests errored, and purges failed. A later bad update briefly restarted the API impact.

title: Hidden transaction pile-up starves Go DB pools and times out API
trigger: Many short-lived database transactions, including a needless one opened on most Slack modal submissions, held connections in the Go database/sql pools.
impact: Over about two weeks, some API requests timed out intermittently while waiting up to around 20 seconds for a connection, with each episode clearing in about a minute; request counts are not given.
detection: A customer report and a spike of context canceled errors in Sentry, followed by Grafana dashboards and traces showing time spent waiting on the pool.
fix: The team added a one-second lock timeout, moved Slack event handling to async PubSub, built per-operation connection-hold metrics, and finally removed the unnecessary transaction so only code needing atomicity opens one.
summary: In early 2023 incident.io saw sporadic API timeouts with no obvious cause: no deploys, no traffic spike, no slow query. Traces eventually showed requests waiting on the client-side database/sql connection pool, not on Postgres itself. The culprit was transaction overuse, especially a wrapper that opened a transaction for most Slack modal submissions, which kept connections checked out. Early quick wins like indexes and a materialised view did not help; new instrumentation of connection hold time found the real issue. Exact dates are not stated.

title: Malware steals engineer SSO session, customer secrets exfiltrated
trigger: Malware on an engineer's laptop, undetected by antivirus, stole a valid 2FA-backed SSO session cookie, letting the attacker impersonate the employee and use their ability to mint production access tokens.
impact: On December 22, 2022 the attacker took customers' stored secrets from production databases, including environment variables and credentials for outside services, and pulled encryption keys from a running process; under 5 customers had reported resulting unauthorized access when the report was published.
detection: A customer flagged suspicious GitHub OAuth activity on December 29, 2022, which led to a joint review with GitHub that uncovered the intrusion.
fix: CircleCI cut off the compromised employee, narrowed production access, rebuilt all production hosts, revoked Project and Personal API Tokens, rotated GitHub OAuth and Bitbucket tokens, told every customer to rotate all stored secrets, and added MDM/antivirus detection plus step-up authentication for production access.
summary: A CircleCI engineer's laptop was infected with malware on December 16, 2022, which stole a 2FA-backed SSO session cookie. Using that session, the attacker escalated into production, ran reconnaissance on December 19 and exfiltrated customer environment variables, API keys and OAuth tokens on December 22, along with encryption keys taken from memory. A customer's report of odd GitHub OAuth use started the investigation. CircleCI revoked Project and Personal API Tokens, rotated GitHub and Bitbucket tokens, rebuilt hosts and urged all customers to rotate every secret stored on the platform.

title: Poison-pill Pub/Sub message repeatedly crashes incident.io Go app
trigger: A Pub/Sub message for a welcome-message subscription caused a panic in a goroutine spawned by the Google Cloud Pub/Sub client, where the existing recover() did not reach.
impact: The app was down for 13 minutes within a 32-minute window (15:40 to 16:12 GMT), with Heroku reporting H10 App crashed errors.
detection: Heroku H10 errors paged the on-call engineer through PagerDuty.
fix: The team purged subscriptions holding unacknowledged messages and disabled non-critical async features, then added recover() to the shared Pub/Sub handler and split web, worker and cron into separate Heroku dyno tiers.
summary: incident.io ran web, worker and cron code in one Go binary on Heroku. A message that crashed its handler kept being redelivered by GCP Pub/Sub, and because the client's Receive runs handlers in fresh goroutines, the panic escaped recovery and killed the whole process, so the app crash-looped. Diagnosis was slow because Heroku dropped the huge goroutine dump, log rate limits hid lines before each crash, and Sentry never got the error. Purging subscriptions stopped the crashes.

title: Internal service exhausts global Filestore API quota for all customers
trigger: A malfunctioning internal Google service that manages many GCP projects flooded the Cloud Filestore API with requests and used up a global request limit.
impact: Customers in every region got HTTP 429 errors on read-only Filestore calls such as List and GetOperation via Console, gcloud and the API for about three hours (07:30 to 10:42 US/Pacific), with no workaround.
detection: Automated alerts paged Google engineers at 07:47 US/Pacific, about nine minutes after the incident began.
fix: Engineers manually paused the misbehaving internal service, and follow-ups aim to remove the global quotas and improve alerting on internal limits.
summary: Cloud Filestore protects itself with a single global cap on API requests. When an internal Google backend that manages a large fleet of projects went haywire and hammered the API, it consumed that shared cap, so Filestore throttled everyone. For roughly three hours, customers worldwide saw 429 errors on read operations like ListInstances in the Console and gcloud, although create and update calls still worked. Recovery came only after engineers shut the internal service down by hand.

title: Schema cache lock contention crash-loops Honeycomb ingest for hours
trigger: The original trigger was never identified; Shepherd ingest hosts entered a persistent loop of running out of memory and restarting.
impact: Ingest was disrupted for more than eight and a half hours in total, and the team estimates that most customers ingesting during that window saw at least partial impact.
detection: Engineers recognized a familiar shark fin pattern in latency graphs, but unlike past episodes it did not clear within about 15 minutes.
fix: Engineers reduced lock contention in the schema cache and pre-filled it before Shepherd hosts took traffic, then added Refinery capacity; longer-term work targets cache contention and ingest re-architecture.
summary: Honeycomb's Shepherd edge hosts validate incoming events against an in-memory schema cache whose updates took a table-wide lock, so backfilling a missing entry stalled unrelated requests. On September 8 Shepherds fell into a metastable cycle of memory exhaustion and restarts, which also crashed the Refinery cluster sampling their traces. Scaling, slower deploys and aggressive sampling did not help, the autoscaler added hosts in response to crash-loop CPU, and an unpinned chart change redeployed mid-incident. Pre-warming the cache at boot finally stabilized ingest.

title: London heatwave cooling failure powers down part of europe-west2-a
trigger: Several redundant cooling systems, including two chillers, failed simultaneously during record outside temperatures at a data center hosting zone europe-west2-a.
impact: Over roughly a day and a half, about 35% of Compute Engine VMs in the zone were terminated, 38% of zonal Persistent Disk volumes went unavailable, 57% of GKE nodes in the zone dropped out, and dozens of other services including Cloud SQL, Bigtable, BigQuery and Cloud Storage reported errors.
detection: Automated temperature monitoring flagged rising heat in the data center and engineers were paged soon after.
fix: Engineers deliberately powered down part of the zone to protect hardware, shifted load away, then restarted services in sequence after cooling was repaired, with follow-ups to fix zonal failover automation, shed thermal load gradually, and audit cooling equipment globally.
summary: During the July 2022 UK heatwave, chillers at a Google Cloud data center in London failed and temperatures climbed until engineers shut down a portion of zone europe-west2-a. VMs were terminated, disks and GKE nodes became unreachable, and caches in Memorystore were flushed. A legacy Cloud Storage placement scheme put three storage clusters in the same failure domain, and a mistaken routing change briefly blocked replicas in other zones too. Restoring the long tail of instances took many extra hours after cooling returned.

title: BGP policy term reorder withdraws prefixes at 19 Cloudflare sites
trigger: A change to prefix advertisement policies on spine routers in Multi-Colo PoP data centers moved a REJECT-THE-REST term ahead of the site-local terms.
impact: Nineteen data centers carrying about half of Cloudflare's HTTP traffic became unreachable for many users from 06:27 UTC, with all sites working again by 07:42 UTC.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem beyond an internal incident being declared at 06:32 UTC.
fix: Engineers reverted the change, using out-of-band access where needed, and planned MCP-aware rollout testing, a policy redesign that prevents term misordering, and automated commit-confirm rollback.
summary: As part of a BGP communities standardization project, Cloudflare reordered terms in the export policy on spine routers in its newer MCP data centers. A REJECT-THE-REST term now came first, so site-local prefixes stopped being advertised and those locations dropped off the internet. The Multimog load balancer also relied on those prefixes, so smaller clusters got overloaded. Only 4% of locations were hit but they served about 50% of HTTP requests. Recovery was slowed by engineers reverting one another's changes.

title: Stolen Heroku GitHub OAuth tokens used to clone private repos
trigger: An attacker found a Heroku machine account token in an archived private GitHub repository, apparently reached through a third-party integration, and used it to enter Heroku's environment.
impact: The attacker downloaded customers' GitHub integration OAuth tokens, cloned private repos of some customers and parts of Heroku's own source, and also took hashed and salted account passwords plus the configuration variables customers had set for Review Apps and Heroku CI pipelines.
detection: GitHub spotted the suspicious activity on April 12, 2022 and alerted Salesforce's security team the following day.
fix: Heroku disabled the compromised account within three hours, revoked every Dashboard GitHub integration token and blocked new ones, reset customer account passwords on May 5, 2022, privately warned customers whose config vars leaked, and rotated other critical credentials during a production freeze.
summary: On April 7, 2022 an attacker who had pulled a Heroku machine account token from an archived private GitHub repo accessed a Heroku database and downloaded customers' GitHub integration OAuth tokens. With them the actor enumerated and cloned private repositories of some customers and part of Heroku's own code. They also took hashed customer passwords and the settings and secrets customers stored for Review Apps and Heroku CI. GitHub raised the alarm; Heroku revoked all GitHub integration tokens, forced customer password resets, and had affected customers rotate leaked config secrets.

title: Cleanup script deletes 883 Atlassian cloud sites
trigger: A script meant to remove a legacy Insight app was given site IDs instead of app IDs, and the deletion API accepted them without checks.
impact: 883 cloud sites belonging to 775 customers were deleted, taking down Jira, Confluence, Opsgenie, Statuspage and Atlassian Access for those customers for up to 14 days.
detection: Internal monitoring missed it because the deletions used a normal workflow; a customer support ticket arrived 8 minutes after the script started and the incident was confirmed about an hour later.
fix: Atlassian restored sites from point-in-time backups over two restore approaches finishing April 18, blocked bulk site deletion, and committed to universal soft deletes, automated multi-site disaster recovery and better incident communication tooling.
summary: A maintenance script to retire the legacy Insight asset management app was run with cloud site identifiers rather than app identifiers. The deletion API treated them as valid and permanently removed 883 entire customer sites, including contact details needed to reach those customers. Restoring was manual and slow because tooling was built for single-site recovery, so some customers waited two weeks. Atlassian met its one-hour recovery point objective but missed its recovery time objective.

title: Consul agent rollout empties caches, scatter queries swamp Vitess
trigger: A percentage-based Consul agent upgrade restarted agents on cache nodes, and Mcrib replaced each one with an empty memcached node, lowering the hit rate at peak.
impact: Many users could not connect to Slack and client boot calls were slow or failed from just after 6 a.m. Pacific; exact counts and duration are not stated.
detection: Support tickets, internal user reports, and pages to several engineering teams all arrived at roughly the same time.
fix: Slack paused the Consul rollout, throttled client boots, changed the query to fetch only missing data from Vitess replicas, and raised limits as caches refilled; follow-ups moved the query to a channel-sharded table and changed the rollout process.
summary: Restarting Consul agents during an upgrade caused Slack's Mcrib cache control plane to swap in empty memcached nodes. Group DM membership lookups on cache miss became scatter queries across every Vitess shard, because the keyspace was sharded by user. Database load grew faster than the miss rate, queries timed out before refilling the cache, and client retries plus Mcrib's quick node replacement deepened the cascading failure. Boot throttling, raised too fast at first, eventually let the cache recover.

title: DNS config change breaks name resolution in container cluster
trigger: A DNS configuration change deployed at 00:17 UTC contained a defect, believed to be a dnsmasq misconfiguration, that left every service in the container orchestration cluster unable to resolve DNS.
impact: From 00:22 to 03:14 UTC on 15 December 2021, PagerDuty's web UI, mobile app, REST API and Events API in both US and EU regions could not reliably ingest events or send notifications on time; most US function returned by 01:30 and EU by about 02:00.
detection: Internal monitoring flagged the problem within one minute.
fix: Engineers deployed a fix to a subset of production, verified it, then rolled it out region by region, and planned stronger pre-deploy config testing and better canaries.
summary: PagerDuty pushed a DNS configuration change to the infrastructure behind its container orchestration cluster, and a defect missed in test environments, likely in dnsmasq settings, stopped all containerised services from resolving hostnames. Event ingestion, notification delivery, the web and mobile UIs and the REST API degraded at once in both US and EU service regions for nearly three hours. Monitoring caught it within a minute; a corrected config was canaried and then rolled out sequentially with verification.

title: Latent load balancer bug breaks Google Front End in Europe
trigger: A newly enabled infrastructure feature activated a latent bug in internal network load balancer code used by Google Front End load balancing.
impact: For about 1 hour 44 minutes (00:30 to 02:14 US/Pacific), mostly European customers could not load Cloud Console and saw failures in Container Registry, Bigtable, Spanner, Endpoints, Cloud SQL, Eventarc and App Engine, with some spillover to us-central1; no customer counts are given.
detection: Automated safety systems caught the errors within about 4 minutes and slowed the rollout.
fix: Engineers pushed a change that disabled the vulnerable code path, and a root cause fix was scheduled to finish rolling out later the same day.
summary: Google Front End, the load balancing layer in front of many Google Cloud services, failed in Europe after a new infrastructure feature exercised a dormant bug in internal network load balancer code. Customers saw the Cloud Console time out, Container Registry API connections fail, Bigtable and Spanner return unavailable errors, and Cloud Run, Cloud Functions and App Engine drop traffic. Automated safety checks noticed within minutes; disabling the buggy code path mitigated the outage after about 1 hour 44 minutes.

title: Incompatible schema change leaves CircleCI jobs stuck not running
trigger: An 18:50 UTC deploy changed a column type in the work distribution database in a way that was not backwards compatible.
impact: Jobs on all executor types sat stuck without starting for about 53 minutes, with queue times staying elevated until 20:19 UTC, especially for machine and Mac executors.
detection: Errors and alerts fired right after the deploy, with error counts spiking and incoming work falling off.
fix: After a rollback failed to help, engineers hand-deployed a change making the distributor ignore the bad field and scaled compute manually, and planned better testing and tolerant handling of unexpected data.
summary: A CircleCI deploy altered a field type in the PostgreSQL database behind its job distribution service. Both new and older work items then broke distribution, and because the distributor halts on bad data and restarts from the beginning, it looped on the same records. Rolling back made rows written in between unreadable, so jobs could not start for nearly an hour. A manual patch to skip the field restored flow, but node health checks and provider rate limits slowed the catch-up.

title: 73-hour Roblox outage from Consul streaming contention and BoltDB
trigger: A newly enabled Consul streaming feature, extended a day earlier to a traffic-routing service, caused heavy contention under high read and write load, compounded by a BoltDB freelist performance problem.
impact: Roblox was fully down for 73 hours from October 28 to October 31, 2021, with no user data lost.
detection: Engineers noticed degraded Vault performance and one Consul server with high CPU, before players were affected.
fix: Streaming was disabled, slow Consul leaders were kept from staying elected, BoltDB was later compacted, and players were let back in via DNS steering; follow-ups removed the telemetry dependency on Consul and added a second datacenter and dedicated Consul clusters.
summary: Roblox depends on a single Consul cluster for service discovery, which Nomad and Vault also rely on. KV write latency jumped from under 300ms to about 2 seconds, and online players fell to half before the whole platform went offline. Swapping hardware, restoring a snapshot and shedding load did not help. Profiling traced kernel spin-lock contention to Consul streaming, and HashiCorp later found BoltDB writing a 7.8MB freelist on each Raft append. Monitoring that depended on Consul made triage harder.

title: Maintenance command severs Facebook backbone; DNS withdraws BGP routes
trigger: A routine maintenance command meant to measure global backbone capacity disconnected every backbone link, and a bug in the audit tool failed to block it.
impact: Facebook services were unreachable worldwide; the postmortem does not give user counts or total duration.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Engineers physically went to data centers to restore the backbone, then brought services back gradually using storm drill practice, and planned to add backbone outage scenarios to future drills.
summary: During routine maintenance, a command to assess Facebook's backbone capacity accidentally took down all backbone connections, cutting data centers off from each other and the internet. An audit tool should have rejected the command but had a bug. Edge DNS servers, unable to reach the data centers, withdrew their BGP advertisements, so Facebook's authoritative name servers vanished from the internet. Internal tools also relied on DNS and out-of-band access was down, so engineers had to work on site, slowed by security controls.

title: Deleted Azure AD group de-provisions all users from GitHub org
trigger: While re-inviting one employee, an admin deleted the Azure Active Directory security group behind GitHub SCIM provisioning instead of removing the user from it.
impact: Employees lost access to the trivago GitHub organization for at least 1 hour 19 minutes and had to accept new invites and re-enable SSH keys and tokens for SSO.
detection: Users reported lost access in Slack within four minutes, and the owning team found the group missing at 16:23.
fix: A new group was created, admins were assigned to the enterprise app directly, and users found via provisioning logs and mail traces were re-added; follow-ups include automated group membership backups and tighter permissions for destructive actions.
summary: trivago syncs GitHub organization membership from an Azure AD security group via SAML SSO and SCIM. After 2FA enforcement removed some accounts, re-inviting one user meant removing and re-adding them to the group, but the whole group was deleted by mistake. SCIM then de-provisioned every synced user from GitHub and sent removal emails. AAD groups cannot be restored, so the team used a sync bot account to restore admins, rebuilt the group, and relied on GitHub to restore previous repository permissions.

title: Honeycomb retro on a run of scaling incidents after ingest growth
trigger: Ingest volume grew around 40% in a few weeks, pushing Kafka, the Beagle SLO processor, retrievers and the dogfood environment past previously unknown limits at the same time.
impact: Over September and early October there were five public incidents and more than 20 internal issues, including user-visible data delays of up to about five minutes and an SLO processing outage.
detection: Problems surfaced through redundant alerting, cross-environment component alerts and Beagle's own warnings that it was falling behind.
fix: The team vertically scaled Kafka brokers, tuned Beagle consumer buffers, fixed a runbook typo, and committed to mapping system limits and revisiting each component's scaling model.
summary: This review covers a cluster of Honeycomb incidents driven by fast ingest growth. Kafka brokers hit AWS network allowance limits and were moved to bigger instances; Beagle, which processes SLO data, autoscaled on CPU, a poor signal, and slowed when the Sarama Kafka client shared one connection per broker leader. A retriever scale-up runbook, never tested in production, inserted an SLO record with an underscore instead of a hyphen in a topic name, crash-looping Beagle and causing a public SLO delay outage.

title: Postgres sequence caching makes incident numbers skip by 32
trigger: The team upgraded its database by promoting a follower to primary, and the new primary resumed Postgres sequences up to 32 values ahead.
impact: A significant share of organizations saw gaps of 32 in their customer-facing INC incident numbers, for example jumping from INC-7 to INC-39; no data was lost or misattributed.
detection: Customers reported the skipped numbers, and the team then audited the database and its sequences.
fix: Per-organization sequences were replaced by a before-insert trigger that sets the external ID to the organization's current maximum plus one, backed by an index.
summary: Customers of incident.io noticed their incident identifiers jumping unexpectedly, such as a team with 20 incidents whose newest was numbered 52. The cause was Postgres sequence behaviour: values are pre-logged in blocks of 32, so after a crash or a follower promotion the new primary can start further ahead. A recent database upgrade via failover triggered exactly that. The team switched to computing the next number with a trigger and recommends keeping user-visible IDs separate from internal keys. The exact incident date is not given.

title: Latent bug triggered by one customer config takes down Fastly edge
trigger: A customer pushed a legitimate configuration change that hit a dormant bug introduced by a Fastly software release rolled out starting May 12.
impact: Around 85% of the Fastly network served errors worldwide from 09:47 UTC; most services were back within about 49 minutes and the incident was mitigated at 12:35 UTC.
detection: Fastly monitoring spotted the global disruption at 09:48 UTC, one minute after onset.
fix: Engineers identified and disabled the triggering customer configuration, then began deploying a permanent code fix at 17:25 UTC and committed to reviewing why testing missed the bug.
summary: A software deployment Fastly started on May 12 carried a hidden bug that only fired under a specific customer configuration. On June 8 a customer made a valid config change matching those conditions, and roughly 85% of Fastly's global CDN began returning errors, knocking many large websites offline. Monitoring caught it within a minute, the offending config was found at 10:27 UTC and disabled, most traffic recovered by 11:00, and a permanent fix rolled out that evening.

title: RabbitMQ upgrade strands VM cleanup queue, blocking CircleCI jobs
trigger: A routine RabbitMQ upgrade introduced a consumer acknowledgment timeout that, contrary to the changelog, applied to all queue types and disconnected consumers of the VM deletion queue.
impact: Docker, machine executor and remote Docker jobs were delayed or blocked for about 12 hours, from 13:30 UTC on May 21 to 01:18 UTC on May 22, and some workflows were cancelled to free resources.
detection: An overnight alert for a queue with zero consumers led only to pod restarts, a later backlog alert was misconfigured and did not page, and the incident was declared after job-start-delay pages at 13:00 UTC.
fix: Engineers obtained a GCP quota increase, manually deleted old VMs, restored queue consumers, scaled up RDS and brought components back one at a time, then planned more robust provisioning, better RabbitMQ observability and batched GCP API calls.
summary: After CircleCI upgraded RabbitMQ, a new acknowledgment timeout kicked consumers off the queue responsible for destroying finished VMs. With nobody consuming it, old VMs piled up and saturated GCP CPU quotas, so new jobs could not get machines, and automatic retries added load. RDS databases then ran out of burst balance, causing connection and I/O failures. Docker, Windows, macOS, Arm and GPU jobs were delayed or stuck for roughly half a day.

title: Overloaded AWS Transit Gateway drops packets on post-holiday Monday
trigger: A surge of returning users with cold client caches overloaded an AWS Transit Gateway that did not scale fast enough, causing packet loss across Slack's VPCs.
impact: Slack became unavailable around 7:00 AM PST on January 4, 2021, stayed degraded after 9:15 AM, and network conditions were normal again by 10:40 AM PST.
detection: An external monitoring service paged on-call as error rates climbed, and Slack's own dashboards and alerting then failed because they depended on the same Transit Gateways.
fix: Slack disabled autoscaling downscaling and repaired provision-service while AWS manually raised Transit Gateway capacity; follow-ups include pre-holiday TGW upscaling requests, colocating monitoring with its databases, and load testing provision-service.
summary: On the first workday of 2021, Slack's traffic spike saturated an AWS Transit Gateway, and the resulting packet loss slowed calls from the web tier to backends. Failing health checks and autoscaling tried to start about 1,200 servers in 15 minutes, but provision-service, on the same degraded network, hit a Linux open-files limit and an AWS quota. Monitoring dashboards lived in a separate VPC from their databases and went dark. Load balancer panic mode and retries kept some traffic flowing.

title: Kinesis front-end capacity add exceeds OS thread limit in us-east-1
trigger: A small capacity addition to the Kinesis Data Streams front-end fleet pushed every front-end server past the operating system thread limit.
impact: Kinesis put and get calls failed in US-EAST-1 for roughly five hours, and dependent services such as Cognito, CloudWatch, Lambda, Auto Scaling, EventBridge, ECS and EKS saw errors or delays, with some not fully recovered until mid-afternoon.
detection: Alarms on Kinesis put and get record errors fired at 5:15 AM PST.
fix: AWS removed the new capacity, changed front-end servers to bootstrap shard maps from the authoritative metadata store and restarted the fleet gradually, then planned larger servers, thread alarms, higher OS limits and a dedicated shard-map cache fleet.
summary: Each Kinesis front-end server keeps threads open to every other front-end server to build its shard-map cache. Adding a few servers raised the per-host thread count beyond an OS limit, so cache construction failed and servers could not route requests to back-end clusters. Kinesis errors spread to CloudWatch, Cognito, Lambda and others, and even status page updates stalled because the posting tool relied on Cognito. Recovery was slow because servers could only rejoin a few hundred per hour.

title: Local reset script drops the production database
trigger: A developer helper function meant to drop and recreate local tables ran against the production database during late-night coding, for reasons the author had not yet determined.
impact: Every scoreboard and its data was wiped; the site was down about 30 minutes, and roughly 7 hours of scoreboard data created on 17 October 2020 was permanently lost.
detection: The developer realised immediately because the function was run by hand; no monitoring is described.
fix: The site went into maintenance mode and was restored from DigitalOcean's daily managed backup, and the team concluded such a destructive function should not exist.
summary: Keepthescore, a small online scoreboard side project, lost its production PostgreSQL data when a Python helper that drops and recreates tables, hardcoded to connect to localhost, somehow wiped production instead. Around 10:45pm CET every scoreboard disappeared. The site was put into maintenance mode and restored from DigitalOcean's once-daily managed database backup within about 30 minutes, but scores entered between 15:47 and 23:21 CET that day were gone for good. The root cause of the wrong connection was still unknown.

title: DNS query flood topples Datadog's service discovery in US region
trigger: Scaling a small latency-measuring cluster down and up left it briefly missing, and a large intake cluster flooded service discovery with repeated DNS lookups for it.
impact: The US region was degraded from 14:27 UTC on September 24, with web tier error rates of about 60-90% and services recovering between 20:18 UTC and 03:00 UTC the next day.
detection: Engineers noticed intermittent intake cluster failures and opened an internal incident a few minutes later.
fix: The service discovery team isolated the cluster and readmitted clients gradually while other teams switched to static local config, with plans to split control and data planes and cache discovery queries.
summary: A Datadog migration had quietly switched an intake cluster from a local hosts file to a local DNS resolver that does not cache NXDOMAIN answers. When a small latency-measuring cluster was briefly removed, intake clients kept re-querying it, multiplying DNS load tenfold in ten seconds. The consensus-based service discovery cluster lost quorum, and as caches expired a thundering herd followed, so services could not find dependencies or load runtime configuration. Dashboards and APIs failed for hours though incoming data kept being ingested.

title: Failed EBS volume on file server takes hosted sites offline
trigger: An AWS EBS volume behind the oldest file server, livefile1, suffered multiple component failures that stalled its redundant disk array.
impact: Websites, scheduled tasks and always-on tasks for the roughly 20% of accounts on livefile1 were down for about three to nearly four hours, and nearly all users were affected at some point because the main site slowed and other sites could not be reloaded.
detection: Monitoring paged the support team at 16:06 UTC with alerts from multiple machines.
fix: The team rebuilt the file server volumes from backup snapshots, cleared stale NFS mounts with a rolling cluster reboot, and planned to script storage rebuilds, detect hung volumes faster, and contain failures to one file server's users.
summary: One of PythonAnywhere's NFS file servers lost its underlying AWS EBS storage when a volume failed in a way AWS later confirmed was unrecoverable. Web app worker processes blocked waiting on storage, so the PythonAnywhere site itself became slow and threw errors, and users across the platform could not start or reload web apps. Engineers restored the volumes from snapshots, then rebooted servers to clear hung NFS mounts. No data was lost, but restored volumes stayed slow for hours while they warmed up.

title: Cooling control system bug overheats servers in a Tokyo AZ
trigger: During a control host failover, a bug in third-party datacenter control software flooded devices with traffic, the system hung, and cooling units shut down instead of falling back to maximum cooling.
impact: A small share of EC2 servers in part of one AP-NORTHEAST-1 Availability Zone overheated and shut down from 12:36 PM JST, degrading EBS and dependent services like RDS, Redshift and ElastiCache, with most recovered by 6:30 PM JST and some hardware retired.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Operators manually reset the control equipment and PLCs and forced maximum cooling, restoring cooling by 3:21 PM JST, then disabled the failover mode and changed controls so purge mode can bypass the PLCs.
summary: In the AWS Tokyo Region, the datacenter control system that manages cooling was failing over between hosts when a bug in vendor logic caused excessive device communication and the system became unresponsive. Air handlers in part of one Availability Zone shut off rather than going to safe maximum cooling, and the manual purge fallback also failed because PLCs hung. EC2 servers overheated, EBS volumes slowed, RunInstances calls errored, and some multi-AZ ALB users with WAF or sticky sessions saw extra errors.

title: WAF regex with catastrophic backtracking pins CPU globally
trigger: A new WAF Managed Rule for XSS was pushed globally at once and included a regular expression prone to catastrophic backtracking, which pinned CPU on the edge.
impact: CPU on every server handling HTTP and HTTPS spiked to nearly 100% worldwide, so customer sites returned 502 errors for about 27 minutes and the dashboard and API were also unreachable.
detection: External synthetic WAF tests failed and paged on-call about three minutes after the deploy, followed by a global traffic-drop alert and reports of CPU exhaustion.
fix: Engineers ran a global WAF kill, then re-enabled it after testing in one location, and followed up by restoring a removed CPU safeguard, auditing all rules for backtracking, adding performance tests, staged rule rollouts and a move to re2 or Rust regex.
summary: A WAF Managed Rule meant to detect cross-site scripting was deployed to Cloudflare's entire edge in one step. Its regular expression caused catastrophic backtracking, and although the rule was in simulate mode it still ran, consuming every CPU core serving HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Sites behind Cloudflare returned 502 errors and the dashboard was down too. A previously removed CPU-limit protection would have contained it. A global WAF termination restored traffic in about 27 minutes.

title: Maintenance automation deschedules network control plane in US regions
trigger: A bug in maintenance automation descheduled network control plane jobs across several physical locations at once, and after a few minutes of fail-static operation BGP routes between those sites were withdrawn.
impact: For about four hours, six GCP regions including us-central1 and us-east1 saw heavy congestion: Cloud Storage errors reached 96% in us-west2, Spanner was down in three regions, Compute Engine saw up to 33% packet loss, and Interconnect saw 50-100% loss.
detection: Engineers were paged two minutes after the failure began, but debugging was slowed because monitoring tools ran over the same congested network.
fix: Engineers halted the automation, rebuilt lost control plane configuration and restored capacity, then hardened cluster management to reject multi-location deschedules, made the control plane persist its config and lengthened fail-static time.
summary: Maintenance automation meant for one location had a bug that let it deschedule logical clusters in several locations together, and the network control plane jobs there were configured to stop during maintenance. The network ran in fail-static mode briefly, then BGP routes were withdrawn and capacity collapsed. Compute Engine, App Engine, Cloud VPN, Interconnect, Pub/Sub, Spanner, Cloud Storage and BigQuery all degraded in several US and South American regions. Recovery was slow because control plane config had been lost and monitoring shared the congested network.

title: Expired signing certificate disables Firefox add-ons
trigger: The intermediate certificate used to sign Firefox add-ons was allowed to expire because its owners believed Firefox did not check expiration dates.
impact: Add-ons stopped working for many Firefox users; the post gives no user counts or exact duration, and fixes rolled out over weeks through eight system add-on versions and six dot releases.
detection: Not stated in the postmortem.
fix: Mozilla pushed a fix through the Studies (Normandy) system and later dot releases, and committed to documenting certificate behaviour, testing expiry and future dates in QA, and building a fast update channel independent of Telemetry.
summary: In 2019 the certificate that signs Firefox add-ons expired, and Firefox rejected extensions it could no longer verify.
